analysis.one_liner: Makes it illegal for manufacturers to force stores to sell their products above a set minimum price.
analysis.headline: A bill to ban manufacturer-enforced minimum retail prices died in the Senate Judiciary Committee without ever getting a vote before the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In June 2007, the Supreme Court ruled 5-4 in Leegin that a manufacturer agreeing with a retailer on a minimum sales price is no longer automatically illegal. This bill would restore the old rule from 1911 to 2007: any agreement between a manufacturer and a retailer, wholesaler, or distributor setting a floor price below which the product cannot be sold would violate the Sherman Act. The bill's findings cite Justice Department and Federal Trade Commission studies finding that states that allowed such price floors had retail prices 18 to 27 percent higher, and that minimum-price agreements generally raised prices. The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, who would keep the ability to buy at discount prices, and discount retailers, which could keep undercutting price floors without being cut off by the manufacturers whose goods they sell. The bill's own findings say the earlier ban 'promoted price competition and the practice of discounting all to the substantial benefit of consumers.'

how_it_helps.text: Restores the per se rule that any manufacturer-retailer agreement setting a minimum sales price violates the Sherman Act, undoing the Supreme Court's June 2007 Leegin decision.

The bill's findings cite Justice Department studies from the late 1960s showing retail prices were 18 to 27 percent higher in states that allowed vertical price fixing, and a 1983 FTC study finding resale price maintenance generally raised prices.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name manufacturers, which would lose the power to enforce minimum prices and punish discounters by cutting off supply. Small specialty retailers that rely on manufacturer-enforced price floors to protect their margins against big discounters would also bear some of the cost.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name manufacturers and some small retailers

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes an automatic ban with no exceptions: even an agreement that genuinely helped a small store offer service or stay in business against a big discounter would be illegal, because the bill says any minimum-price agreement 'shall violate' the Sherman Act.

Economists who supported the Leegin decision argue that minimum-price agreements can be pro-competitive in some cases — for example, letting a specialty store recoup the cost of demonstrations and advice, or letting new brands recruit committed retailers — and that a blanket ban throws out those cases along with the harmful ones. The bill rejects that view by statute rather than case by case.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main gain goes to ordinary shoppers, and the studies cited in the bill suggest minimum-price agreements raise prices more often than they help. The cost falls on manufacturers and on a class of retailers that depends on protected margins. The weakness is the bill's one-size-fits-all approach: it re-imposes a blanket ban rather than letting courts sort agreements that raise prices from those that do not. On balance it is a consumer-protection bill, but a blunt one.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate on October 30, 2007, read twice, and referred to the Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: The Supreme Court's June 2007 Leegin decision, a 5-4 ruling, overturned a 96-year-old rule that had made manufacturer-enforced minimum retail prices automatically illegal.
Senator Kohl introduced this bill on October 30, 2007 to reverse that ruling by statute, with three Democratic cosponsors.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee; no further action was ever taken on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name manufacturers, which kept the power to enforce minimum retail prices after Leegin, and the small and specialty retailers whose margins those price floors protect. Consumers and discounters lost the statutory protection the bill would have restored.

for.name: Herb Kohl
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-WI); Chairman, Senate Judiciary Antitrust Subcommittee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on October 30, 2007 to restore the per se ban on resale price maintenance.

against.name: Patrick Leahy
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup or floor action on the bill; it sat in committee for the rest of the 110th Congress.

against.name: Brand-name manufacturers and their trade associations
against.role: Manufacturers seeking to keep minimum resale price enforcement after the Leegin decision
against.what_they_did: Opposed legislation to restore the per se ban on resale price maintenance, arguing minimum-price agreements can be pro-competitive.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Democrat with three Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support recorded; it never reached a vote, so no roll-call shows where the parties stood.

industries.note: The bill strips manufacturers of the power to set minimum prices and cut off discounters, a power the Leegin ruling had just restored. Their gain from the bill's failure comes at the price consumers pay at the register.
The bill protects the ability to discount below manufacturer-set floors, which is how large discounters compete on price. Their interest lines up with consumers'.

Manufacturer-enforced price floors can protect a small store's margins and its ability to offer service, but they do it by keeping the lowest prices off the market. A per se ban removes that protection.
